clinicalPearls: Thyroid nodules are common: ~3-7% of adults by palpation, but up to 50% have nodules on ultrasound, with the majority <1 cm. The vast majority of nodules are benign (Harrison 22e p.3040, p.3044, p.3048).

Initial workup of a nodule begins with a TSH level. If TSH is suppressed, a radionuclide scan is done; a hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodule is almost never malignant, so FNA is unnecessary. Otherwise proceed to thyroid ultrasound (Harrison 22e p.3048).

Thyroid ultrasound with a validated risk-stratification system (e.g., ACR TI-RADS, TR1-TR5) is used to decide which nodules need fine-needle aspiration (FNA), combining sonographic pattern with nodule size; more suspicious patterns warrant FNA at lower size cutoffs (Harrison 22e p.3042, p.3048).

FNA, ideally ultrasound-guided, is the diagnostic procedure of choice for nodules. Cytology is reported with the six-tier Bethesda System (version 3): benign ~4% malignancy risk, AUS ~22%, follicular neoplasm ~30%, suspicious for malignancy ~74%, malignant ~97% (Harrison 22e p.3044, p.3049).

Papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) is the most common type (80-85% of well-differentiated cancers); classic and follicular variants are usually indolent, spread mainly via lymphatics, and have an excellent prognosis (>95% present at stage I or II) (Harrison 22e p.3046).

Follicular thyroid cancer (FTC) accounts for ~5% of US thyroid cancers and cannot be distinguished from benign follicular lesions by FNA cytology alone; diagnosis requires histologic evidence of capsular and/or vascular invasion (Harrison 22e p.3046-3047, p.3048).

Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) arises from calcitonin-producing C cells, accounts for ~5% of thyroid cancers, and can be sporadic or familial (MEN 2A, MEN 2B, familial MTC); elevated serum calcitonin is a marker of residual/recurrent disease (Harrison 22e p.3048).

All patients with MTC should be tested for RET mutations so that genetic counseling and family testing can be offered; pheochromocytoma must be excluded before surgery in any patient with a RET mutation (Harrison 22e p.3048).
Anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC) is poorly differentiated and aggressive with a bleak prognosis; most patients die within 6 months of diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3040, p.3048).

Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is a sensitive marker of residual/recurrent disease for PTC, FTC, and oncocytic carcinoma after total thyroidectomy and radioablation, while calcitonin serves this role for MTC (Harrison 22e p.3045, p.3047).

Molecular diagnostic panels (next-generation sequencing, microRNA, gene expression) are increasingly used on FNA samples with indeterminate cytology (AUS, follicular neoplasm) to distinguish benign from malignant lesions and reduce unnecessary diagnostic surgery; current validated tests have negative predictive values >95% (Harrison 22e p.3046, p.3050).
harrison.pathophysiology: Thyroid nodular disease reflects disordered growth of thyroid cells that may be hyperplastic or neoplastic. Thyroid neoplasms can arise from follicular cells (papillary, follicular, oncocytic, poorly differentiated, anaplastic carcinomas), calcitonin-producing C cells (medullary carcinoma), lymphocytes (lymphoma), or stromal/vascular elements. Cancers are monoclonal, arising from mutations conferring a growth advantage or resistance to cell death. Activation of the RET-RAS-BRAF (MAPK) signaling pathway is seen in up to 70% of PTCs; BRAF V600E mutations occur in up to 60% of PTC, RET rearrangements in ~15% (more frequent after Chernobyl fallout), and RAS mutations in ~15%. FTCs harbor BRAF/RAS mutations plus PAX8-PPARgamma rearrangements (~70% have a mutation/rearrangement). Anaplastic cancers accumulate additional TERT promoter, BRAF, CTNNB1 (beta-catenin), and TP53 mutations driving dedifferentiation and genetic instability. MEN 2-associated MTC carries inherited activating RET point mutations and is preceded by C-cell hyperplasia. External and fallout radiation predispose to chromosomal breaks and increase risk of benign and malignant nodules, especially in children. Most differentiated cancers retain TSH receptor expression and respond to TSH, the basis for both LT4 suppression and radioiodine uptake.

harrison.prognosis: Prognosis spans a wide range by histologic type. Differentiated cancers (PTC and FTC) are often curable with good prognosis in early-stage disease; the 20-year disease-specific mortality for low-risk thyroid cancer is ~1%, and most PTC present at stage I/II with survival similar to expected. Mortality rises markedly in stage IV disease, especially with distant metastases (stage IVB, ~1% of patients). FTC, particularly angioinvasive, carries less favorable outcomes than PTC partly due to more stage IV presentation; poor features include distant metastases, age >55, tumor >4 cm, and marked vascular invasion. MTC is more aggressive in MEN 2B than MEN 2A, and familial MTC more aggressive than sporadic. Anaplastic thyroid cancer is aggressive with a bleak prognosis, most patients dying within 6 months. Older age (>65) and male gender are associated with worse outcomes overall.
pitfalls: Thyroid cancer is being overdiagnosed: rising incidence is driven by small T1 papillary tumors while disease-specific mortality has not changed in 40 years; routine FNA is not recommended for nodules <1 cm unless metastatic cervical nodes are present.
A hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodule on radionuclide scan is almost never malignant; FNA is unnecessary and should not be performed for these.

FNA cytology cannot reliably distinguish benign follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma because nuclear features do not differ; the distinction requires histologic evidence of capsular/vascular invasion.

LT4 (TSH-suppression) therapy does NOT shrink nodules in iodine-replete (iodine-sufficient) populations and should not be used for that purpose; if it has not reduced nodule size after 6-12 months it should be stopped.
Spongiform nodules (TR1) have <3% cancer risk and warrant observation rather than FNA.
Iodine-containing contrast agents should be avoided in nodular goiter due to the risk of the Jod-Basedow effect (iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis from autonomous nodules).
NIFTP can only be diagnosed on surgical pathology, so it is still included within Bethesda malignancy risk estimates.
Hoarseness more commonly reflects benign causes (e.g., reflux) than malignancy, but new vocal cord paralysis is a genuine red flag.
In MTC, surgery should not proceed until pheochromocytoma has been excluded in any patient with a RET mutation.
For thyroid lymphoma, initial surgical resection should be avoided because it may spread otherwise localized disease.
harrison.severityClassification: Histologic classification (WHO/Table 397-1): follicular cell-derived (benign follicular/oncocytic adenoma; low-risk neoplasms including NIFTP; malignant - papillary, follicular, oncocytic, differentiated/poorly differentiated high-grade, anaplastic), C-cell-derived medullary carcinoma, mixed medullary-follicular, lymphoma, and others. Staging uses the AJCC/UICC 8th-edition TNM system (tumor size and extrathyroidal invasion, regional nodal metastases, distant metastases) for differentiated and anaplastic cancers. Sonographic risk stratification uses ACR TI-RADS levels TR1 (benign) to TR5 (highly suspicious). FNA cytology uses the six-tier Bethesda System v3 (I nondiagnostic ~13%, II benign ~4%, III AUS ~22%, IV follicular neoplasm ~30%, V suspicious for malignancy ~74%, VI malignant ~97% malignancy risk). MTC risk in MEN 2 is further stratified by specific RET mutation.
management: Surgery is the mainstay for malignant nodules, with lobectomy or total thyroidectomy according to size and risk and lymph-node dissection for nodal disease
Give radioactive iodine ablation of residual differentiated disease after total thyroidectomy in appropriate risk groups
Provide TSH-suppressive levothyroxine for differentiated cancer, with lifelong thyroid hormone replacement after thyroidectomy
Treat medullary carcinoma with total thyroidectomy and central-compartment node dissection, screening for and treating any associated phaeochromocytoma before operating and undertaking RET testing

Manage anaplastic and advanced disease with multimodality chemoradiotherapy and targeted kinase inhibitors such as BRAF and MEK inhibitors for BRAF-mutant tumours or RET inhibitors, often with palliative intent
Offer active surveillance for selected low-risk papillary microcarcinoma and monitor benign nodules
Follow up with serum thyroglobulin and neck ultrasound, using calcitonin and CEA for medullary disease, and manage post-operative hypoparathyroidism and hypocalcaemia
Provide genetic counselling and RET testing for medullary carcinoma and multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes
